doc.title: Steve Turré interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 29, 2021

title: Rhythm and African roots in teaching
summary: Rhythm comes first; jazz taught from a European perspective misses its African root, so he has students play percussion and links swing to African six.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: How do you have them work on that? To get more rhythm in their playing?

Well look it. Let’s make an analogy here. If you’re studying harmony you’ve got to start with the root. And once you have three notes you have a chord and then you build off the top of that. But you go back to the root. So it’s the same thing with rhythm. Let’s go to the root. What makes jazz music different than — you see in academia especially in the United States but in Europe too they teach music, even jazz music, they teach it from a European perspective. And yes most of the instruments are European instruments that have been co-opted because African-Americans weren’t allowed to play their instruments and we used the notation and the harmonic system of European music and it’s not — I’m not putting it down, it’s a beautiful thing, it’s a melding of concepts. But rhythm is still the thing that we use in the harmony and the notation instruments in European music. The thing that differentiates it is at the root of it is African culture. It’s improvisation, call and

response, rhythm is number one. Rhythm. And so you know if I have a student that really has a problem with rhythm I have them pick up some percussion instruments. Learn to play the clave, learn to play a basic rhythm and hold it steady. You’ve got to listen and make it fit like this with the other rhythms. And it breathes. It’s not a metronome like a drum machine. You have to adjust to the ebb and flow of the collective. It’s a collective consciousness. And I put on traditional African drummers and show them where swing comes from, because African six it’s the same thing as swing, if it’s played right. And when I played with Art Blakey and Max Roach, you know, the same thing — the swing feels the same as African six.
